passage: In the colony garden, Nandini announced, "I am the doctor!" and hung her grandmother's old dupatta around her neck like a stethoscope. Sunaina lay on the bench as the patient. Soon other children ran past with a ball, shouting. Sunaina sat up. "Let's play catch now." Nandini frowned. "No. I said I'm the doctor." "But it's boring now." Nandini's lip trembled, but she pressed the dupatta to Sunaina's knee. "Doctors don't stop in the middle." She kept checking the same knee, looking toward the ball game every few seconds.

qa.q: What did Nandini use as a stethoscope?
qa.a: Her grandmother's old dupatta.

qa.q: Why did Nandini keep playing doctor even while looking at the ball game?
qa.a: She felt torn: she had announced "I am the doctor" and going back on it felt wrong, even though she wanted to play catch too, which is why her lip trembled.

qa.q: What could Sunaina or an adult say to help Nandini switch games without feeling she broke her word?
qa.a: They could suggest the doctor finishes the check-up first and then goes to play, so Nandini keeps her word and still joins in.

qa.q: What is it like for Sunaina, lying on the bench while others play catch?
qa.a: Sunaina is bored and wants to join the ball game, and may feel stuck being the patient because Nandini won't change.

grounding: A young girl who announced she is the doctor refuses to change the game even when it stops being fun, because going back on her word feels wrong.

passage:
Classroom note, Wednesday — Salma, nursery teacher
During pretend play, Elizabeth, 5, declared, "I am the doctor, and I'm the doctor all day." The others were happy for a while, then wanted to switch to a shop game. Elizabeth refused. She kept her toy stethoscope on and said, "I said it. I can't change." She sat alone in the clinic corner, watching the shop game, sad but firm. I sat beside her and asked if doctors sometimes buy medicine at shops. She thought about it, then walked over with the stethoscope still on and bought "medicine" from the shop. Note: she seems to feel bound by her own announcements. Offer ways to honour them.

qa.q: What game did the other children want to switch to?
qa.a: A shop game.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth saying "I said it. I can't change" show about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels her spoken word binds her, so changing the game feels wrong even though she is sad sitting alone.

qa.q: What did Salma do that helped Elizabeth join in?
qa.a: She asked if doctors sometimes buy medicine at shops, which let Elizabeth join the shop game while still being the doctor.

qa.q: How might the other children see Elizabeth's refusal?
qa.a: They may be puzzled or a bit annoyed that she won't switch, since they just want to play the new game together.

grounding: A nursery teacher notes a girl who refuses to leave her announced doctor role even when it stops being fun, because changing feels like breaking her word.

passage:
Preschool note, Tuesday. From Rekha, teacher.
In pretend play, Saurabh put on the white coat and said loudly, "I am the doctor today!" He treated three teddies.
By pack-up time, the other children wanted to be bus drivers. Saurabh was the only one left at the clinic corner. He looked tired and his voice was wobbly, but he kept saying, "I'm the doctor. I said it."
What I did next: I told him doctors take the bus home too. He thought, nodded, and climbed on the chair-bus still wearing the coat. He smiled for the first time in twenty minutes.

qa.q: How many teddies did Saurabh treat?
qa.a: He treated three teddies.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh stay at the clinic corner even when tired?
qa.a: He felt upset and bound by his words, because saying "I am the doctor today" made changing feel wrong.

qa.q: Why did Rekha's idea work?
qa.a: Saying doctors take the bus home too let Saurabh join the new game without going back on what he said.

qa.q: How might the other children see Saurabh at the clinic corner?
qa.a: They might think he is just stubborn and wonder why he won't be a bus driver with them.

grounding: A young child who declared he is the doctor keeps playing it alone after it stops being fun, until a teacher lets him keep his word.
